opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most exciting things happening right now is that the size of team needed to build something meaningful is shrinking dramatically. Engineers with access to AI coding assistants can prototype in a day what used to take a week or a month. When a small team can build that quickly, the bottleneck shifts.

What I'm seeing in a lot of teams is that the hard part is no longer writing the code. It's deciding what to build. Product management, talking to users, figuring out what the right feature is, that's becoming the constraint. I've even heard teams joke about flipping the traditional ratio. Instead of one product manager for every six or seven engineers, some teams are moving toward a much higher ratio of product thinking to engineering, because the engineers are so much faster now.

Small teams also have a real advantage in decision speed. If you're two or three people, and you can build a prototype in an afternoon, you can show it to users, get feedback, and iterate the next morning. In a large organization, just getting alignment on whether to try something can take weeks. So the gap between small and large teams, in terms of iteration speed, is widening.

I want to be careful not to overhype it. AI doesn't make every task ten times faster. Writing a quick prototype, maybe yes. Maintaining a large, mission-critical production codebase, the gains are real but more modest, and you still need good engineering judgment, testing, and security discipline. But for exploration and getting to product-market fit, the economics have changed. You can try many more ideas cheaply, throw away the ones that don't work, and double down on the ones that do.

So my advice to founders and teams is: keep the team small and highly skilled, make sure everyone, not just engineers, learns to use these AI tools well, and invest heavily in the skill of quickly figuring out what users actually need. That's where a lot of the leverage is now.

r001.rationale: The response attributes small teams’ advantage both to AI-assisted building and to their general decision speed and faster alignment.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that large technology companies could become more effective by reducing headcount by about 70%.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because the dynamics of building a startup have really changed in the last couple of years.

The way I think about it is, the speed of engineering has gone up dramatically. With AI coding assistants, a small team can now write code maybe two, three, in some cases ten times faster than before. And when the cost of building something drops that much, it changes what the bottleneck is. For a long time, the constraint on a startup was, can you build the thing? Now, increasingly, the constraint is, do you know what to build? Getting product feedback, talking to users, running experiments, making decisions about what to prioritize. Those are now the slow parts.

So one thing I've noticed is that the teams that do really well are the ones where product management and engineering are tightly coupled, or honestly, where the same person is doing both. We used to have a ratio of maybe one PM to four or six engineers. I now sometimes advise teams to flip that, or at least to make sure the engineers have deep empathy for the user, because if engineering is fast and product decisions are slow, you just end up building the wrong thing faster.

The second thing is that small teams have a huge structural advantage in this environment. Communication overhead is low. A team of two or three people can make a decision in an afternoon and have working code the next morning. In a large organization, that same decision might take weeks of alignment meetings. So the leverage from AI tools accrues disproportionately to small, fast, high-trust teams.

And the third thing I'd say is that the skill set is shifting. I think everyone, not just engineers, should learn to code, or at least learn to direct a computer to do what they want. I've seen marketers, salespeople, operations folks at AI Fund who can now write small pieces of software to analyze data or automate a task. That used to require asking an engineer and waiting. Now they just do it. So the "efficiency" is not only that engineers are faster. It's that the pool of people who can build things has gotten much bigger.

I don't think this means large teams go away. There are still problems that need a lot of people. But I do think the minimum viable team for getting a real product in front of real users has shrunk a lot, and that's a very exciting thing for anyone who wants to start something.

r001.rationale: The response says small teams have a structural advantage because communication overhead is low, and that AI’s leverage accrues disproportionately to small, fast teams.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that large technology companies could improve by cutting headcount about 70%; it says large teams are still needed for some problems.

astra-6.text:
I think AI is dramatically reducing the cost of building software, and that gives small teams a lot more leverage. A few people can take an idea, build a prototype, put it in front of users, and learn from it much faster than they could before.

But I’d distinguish writing code faster from making the whole team more effective. If engineering speeds up, but you still spend weeks deciding what to build or waiting for approvals, you haven’t captured much of the benefit. Small teams can be very effective because the person who understands the user may also be the person building the product. That makes the feedback loop much shorter.

So I’d look at how quickly a team can test an idea and deliver something useful. AI helps with implementation, but judgment about what’s worth building remains really important.

r001.rationale: It says small teams can be effective because they shorten the user feedback loop, but does not suggest their AI efficiency partly reflects small-team efficiency in general.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim that large technology companies could improve by cutting headcount by about 70%.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI is making small teams much more capable, but the gains depend on the task. If you have a clear idea of what to build, a few engineers using AI can move very quickly. Writing the code, building a prototype, trying another approach—all of those steps are getting cheaper.

But that shifts the bottleneck. You still have to figure out what users actually need and whether what you built solves their problem. If coding takes a day instead of a week, but you spend a month deciding what to code, you haven’t sped up the whole process very much.

So I’d look at how quickly a team can go from an idea to something a user can try, learn from that interaction, and improve it. That’s where I think small teams have a real advantage: they can combine these tools with very fast decisions and tight feedback loops.

r001.rationale: The response attributes small teams’ advantage partly to fast decisions and tight feedback loops, alongside AI tools, suggesting their efficiency reflects how small teams work generally.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that large technology companies could become more effective by cutting headcount by about 70%.
